- `VStack` (lines 355–395): field `children: Vec<Box<dyn View>>` (line 356); `View::build` (384–395) produces `Node { id: 0, component: Component::VStack, children: self.children.iter().map(|c| c.build()).collect(), ... }` — each child `Box<dyn View>` is collapsed to a `Node` recursively. **This is where `Box<dyn View>` (compile-time view graph) becomes `Vec<Node>` (retained value tree).**
- `HStack` (398–438): identical pattern.
- `Text` (441–466): `text: String`; `build` → `Component::Text { text: clone }`.
- `Spacer` (469–496): unit struct; `build` → `Component::Spacer`.
- `Button` (499–524): `label: String`; `build` → `Component::Button { label: clone }`.
- Free functions: `text(&str)` (112–114), `spacer()` (117–119), `button(&str)` (527–529).

### `vstack!`/`hstack!` macros (lines 94–109)

```rust
macro_rules! vstack {                      // line 95
    ($($child:expr),* $(,)?) => {
        $crate::VStack::new().children($crate::vec![$($crate::Box::new($child)),*])
    };
}
```

`hstack!` is identical (lines 104–109). They box children automatically so children can be heterogeneous (`Text`, `HStack`, `Modified`, custom `View`s). `Box` and `vec!` are re-exported at crate root for hygiene (lines 71, 73).

### `assign_ids` (lines 539–545)

```rust
pub fn assign_ids(root: &mut Node, next: &mut u32) {   // line 539
    root.id = *next;
    *next += 1;
    for child in &mut root.children {
        assign_ids(child, next);                        // line 543
    }
}
```

Pre-order, root first, sequential (test at 666–673: root=1, children=2,3, grandchild=4). The doc comment (lines 536–538) states the contract: **the engine keys its diff snapshot by node id, so call this after building the (possibly re-built) tree and before `Engine::emit`.** Stable ids across rebuilds are the entire basis for diffing.

---

## 2. `pathland-engine` — `crates/pathland-engine/src/lib.rs`

### `SnapshotNode` (lines 60–71)

```rust
struct SnapshotNode {                      // line 61
    component_type: u16,                   // line 62
    parent: Option<u32>,                   // line 63
    index: usize,                          // line 64
    text: Option<String>,                  // line 65
    width: Option<f32>,                    // line 66
    height: Option<f32>,                   // line 67
    properties: BTreeMap<u16, u32>,        // line 68
    gen: u64,                              // line 69  — generation stamp for deletion detection
}
```

This is the **only** state the engine remembers — it is a snapshot of the *last emitted* tree, not the application state.

### `Engine` struct (lines 89–94)

```rust
pub struct Engine {                        // line 89
    snapshot: Vec<Option<SnapshotNode>>,   // line 91  — nodeId → last emitted state (preallocated slab)
    gen: u64,                              // line 93  — monotonic generation stamp for current pass
}
```

`new()` at 103–108; `Default` at 96–100. `tracked_nodes()` diagnostic at 135–137. `slot_mut(id)` (139–145) resizes the slab on demand (allocation only when the tree *grows*).

### `emit()` — diff-based reactive emission (lines 111–132)

```rust
pub fn emit(&mut self, root: &Node, guest: &mut Guest<'_>)
    -> Result<EmitResult, pathland_opcode::RingError> {   // line 111
    self.gen = self.gen.wrapping_add(1);                  // line 116
    let mut out = 0usize;
    self.reconcile_node(root, None, 0, guest, &mut out)?; // line 118
    // Delete sweep: any snapshot slot not visited this pass has stale gen.   // 121–130
    for (id, slot) in self.snapshot.iter_mut().enumerate() {
        if let Some(s) = slot {
            if s.gen != self.gen {
                guest.delete_node(id as u32)?;            // line 125  DELETE_NODE
                *out += 1;
                *slot = None;                             // line 127
            }
        }
    }
    Ok(EmitResult { opcodes: out })                       // line 131
}
```

Algorithm: bump generation → reconcile the passed tree recursively → sweep the snapshot slab for any entry whose generation stamp was not refreshed (i.e., not visited this pass) and emit `DELETE_NODE`. `EmitResult` (lines 78–82) just counts opcodes.

### `reconcile_node` (lines 147–296)

Signature (lines 148–155): `(&mut self, node: &Node, parent: Option<u32>, index: usize, guest: &mut Guest<'_>, out: &mut usize)`.

Preliminaries:
- `component_type = component_type_id(&node.component)` (line 156).
- `text_borrowed`: text of `Text` or label of `Button`, else `None` (lines 158–162).
- `let prev = self.slot_mut(node.id).take()` (line 164) — **pops the previous snapshot entry; `prev == None` means "new node", `prev == Some(p)` means "existing node"**. This is the entire new-vs-existing detection mechanism.
- `props_changed` (165–168) and `text_changed` (170–173) computed without cloning.

**New-node arm (`None`, lines 177–193)** emits, in order:
1. `guest.create_node(node.id, component_type)` → `TREE:CREATE_NODE` (line 178)
2. `guest.insert_child(p, node.id, index)` → `TREE:INSERT_CHILD` (only if parent exists, line 181)
3. Every property: `guest.set_property(node.id, prop, value_type_for(prop), value)` → `STYLE:SET_PROPERTY` (lines 184–187)
4. `emit_size_props` → WIDTH/HEIGHT properties (line 188; helper at 299–324)
5. `guest.set_text(node.id, t)` → `STYLE:SET_TEXT` for Text/Button (lines 189–192)

**Existing-node arm (`Some(p)`, lines 194–255)**, diffed against the snapshot:
1. **Parent moved** (`p.parent != parent`, lines 196–204): emits `REMOVE_CHILD(old, node.id)` if there was an old parent, then `INSERT_CHILD(new, node.id, index)` if there is a new one.
2. **Reordered** (`p.index != index` within same parent, lines 205–210): emits `MOVE_CHILD(par, node.id, index)` → `TREE:MOVE_CHILD`.
3. **Component type changed** (lines 212–215): re-emits `CREATE_NODE` (protocol has no "change type" opcode — the host recreates the element).
4. **Text changed** (lines 217–222): `SET_TEXT`.
5. **Width/height diffs** (lines 224–245): `SET_PROPERTY` with WIDTH/HEIGHT. Note: only the `Some` → `Some` change direction emits; clearing a size (Some → None) emits nothing.
6. **Property map diff** (lines 246–254): iterates `node.properties` and emits `SET_PROPERTY` only for keys where `p.properties.get(prop) != Some(value)`. **Removed properties emit no opcode** (no "unset property" exists in the protocol).

After the match, the new snapshot entry is stored (lines 261–290):
- Zero-alloc optimization: if `props_changed`/`text_changed` were false, the previous `BTreeMap`/`String` allocations are **moved back** into the new `SnapshotNode` (lines 264–271); only changed fields are freshly allocated (273–280). This is what makes steady-state emission allocation-free.
- Snapshot written with `gen: self.gen` (lines 281–290).
- Recursion into children: `reconcile_node(child, Some(node.id), i, ...)` (lines 292–294).

### Does the engine hold a retained tree?

**No.** `Engine` holds only the diff snapshot (`snapshot` slab + `gen`). The caller passes a fresh `&Node` to `emit` on every frame (line 112). The retained tree lives elsewhere:

- In the **native Rust** path: in the application (e.g., a struct holding a `Node` the app mutates and re-passes).
- In the **WASM guest** path (`crates/pathland-guest/src/lib.rs`): the retained tree is a flat id-indexed map `State.nodes: HashMap<u32, FlatNode>` (lines 42–48, 56). Every `emit()` call **re-materializes the entire `Node` tree from scratch** via `materialize(&s.nodes, root_id)` (lines 109–120, called at line 214), then passes it to `engine.emit(&root, &mut ring)`. So the full tree is re-authored from the flat builder state on every emit — the DSL `build()` in the pure-Rust path similarly rebuilds a fresh `Node` from the view structs each time.

### Dependency tracking: **Does not exist**

I searched all crates for `signal|dirty|depend|invalidate|memo|reactive|subscribe`. Findings:

- The **only** hits in `pathland-engine` are doc comments:
  - Lines 15–16: *"This is what signals in the application drive — a signal marks the tree dirty; `emit` reconciles."*
  - Line 84: `/// The diff-based reactive emitter.`
  - These are **aspirational documentation only** — there is no signal type, no `dirty` flag, no dependency graph, no memoization, no invalidation mechanism, no subscription primitive anywhere in the crate (or in `pathland-view`, `pathland-guest`, or the WIT world `wit/pathland.wit`).
- The guest's `builder` interface (`create-node`, `insert-child`, `remove-child`, `set-text`, `set-property`) mutates the flat map with **no change tracking** — `create_node` even unconditionally clears all properties (guest lib.rs lines 135–144).
- `AGENTS.md` confirms this is a known gap: *"Planned / deferred: signals (Goal 2/#13)"*.

**Conclusion**: Reconciliation is **pure tree-to-snapshot structural diffing** of two full trees. There is no link from application state to view nodes. The application (or WIT host) is responsible for (a) detecting that something changed, (b) mutating the retained tree (Node properties / flat map), (c) re-authoring/re-passing the full `&Node`, and (d) calling `emit`. The engine only diff-compares the freshly passed tree against what it last emitted, keyed by stable node ids assigned via `assign_ids` / host-supplied ids. An unchanged tree emits exactly zero opcodes (test, lines 502–512), and steady-state emission provably performs zero heap allocations (test, lines 515–563).

### Opcode coverage summary

The engine emits exactly these protocol commands (constants in `pathland-opcode/src/constants.rs`):
- `TREE:CREATE_NODE` (0x01, line 23), `TREE:DELETE_NODE` (0x02, line 25), `TREE:INSERT_CHILD` (0x03, line 27), `TREE:REMOVE_CHILD` (0x04, line 29), `TREE:MOVE_CHILD` (0x05, line 31)
- `STYLE:SET_PROPERTY` (0x01, line 37), `STYLE:SET_TEXT` (0x03, line 41)
- All funneled through the `Guest` API in `pathland-opcode/src/lib.rs` (lines 151–201).

# Architecture Investigation: Pathland Opcode + Transport + Host

## Summary of the current transport mechanism

There are **two concrete transport paths**, both producing/consuming the same `pathland_opcode::Frame` view type:

1. **Shared linear-memory ring** (local/desktop, zero-copy): `Guest` (producer) writes 16-byte opcodes + arena data into a fixed region of linear memory; `Host` (consumer) drains completed frames. Both live in `pathland-opcode`.
2. **Network batch** (SSR → browser): `BatchEncoder`/`Batcher` serialize opcodes + an **arena delta** into a binary batch; `BatchDecoder` deserializes and mirrors the arena, yielding a `Frame`.

**There is NO transport abstraction trait.** The polymorphism is achieved through a concrete type, `pathland_opcode::Frame` — explicitly documented as "the transport seam" (`lib.rs:227-229`, `transport/src/lib.rs:13-16`). The only traits in the workspace are `pathland-view`'s `View`/`ViewModifier`/`ViewExt`, `pathland-wit-host`'s `AppHandler`, and generated WIT `Guest` world traits. `RenderTree::apply_frame` accepts a `&Frame`, so ring-sourced frames and network-batch frames flow through the identical decode path.

---

## 1. `pathland-opcode` (`crates/pathland-opcode/src/`)

`no_std + alloc`, no runtime dependencies (`Cargo.toml:11`).

### `opcode.rs` — the 16-byte `Opcode`

- **`Opcode` struct** (`opcode.rs:23-38`): `#[repr(C, packed)]`, `#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]`. Fields in wire order:
  - `pub category: u8` (line 27)
  - `pub command: u8` (line 29)
  - `pub flags: u16` (line 31)
  - `pub a: u32` (line 33), `pub b: u32` (line 35), `pub c: u32` (line 37)
- `OPCODE_SIZE: usize = 16` (line 15), `Opcode::SIZE` const (line 42).
- **`new(category, command, flags, a, b, c) -> Self`** (`const fn`, lines 46-55).
- Accessors use `ptr::addr_of!().read_unaligned()` because the struct is packed: `category()` (59-61), `command()` (65-67), `flags()` (71-74), `a()` (78-81), `b()` (85-88), `c()` (92-95). Float reinterpretations `a_f32`/`b_f32`/`c_f32` (99-113).
- **`to_bytes(&self) -> [u8; OPCODE_SIZE]`** (lines 116-130): field 0 = category, 1 = command, then little-endian `flags` at `[2..4]`, `a` at `[4..8]`, `b` at `[8..12]`, `c` at `[12..16]`.
- **`from_bytes(bytes: &[u8; OPCODE_SIZE]) -> Self`** (lines 133-148): byte-slices with `u16/u32::from_le_bytes`.

### `constants.rs` — wire protocol constants

- **Categories** (`category` mod, lines 7-18): `TREE = 0x01`, `STYLE = 0x02`, `EVENT = 0x03`, `META = 0x04`.
- **TREE commands** (`tree` mod, lines 21-32): `CREATE_NODE=0x01`, `DELETE_NODE=0x02`, `INSERT_CHILD=0x03`, `REMOVE_CHILD=0x04`, `MOVE_CHILD=0x05`, each with payload-field docs.
- **STYLE commands** (`style` mod, lines 34-42): `SET_PROPERTY=0x01` (`B=(valueType<<16)|propertyId`), `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN=0x02`, `SET_TEXT=0x03`.
- **EVENT commands** (`event` mod, lines 44-60): `POINTER_DOWN=0x01`, `POINTER_MOVE=0x02`, `POINTER_UP=0x03`, `KEY_DOWN=0x04`, `KEY_UP=0x05`.

The arena is an append-only bump buffer. Each batch carries only bytes appended since the previous batch:

- **Consumer side**: the decoder maintains a mirror `Vec<u8>` and appends each batch's delta (batch.rs:246), clearing it on `RESET` (batch.rs:243-245). [host]  RenderTree.apply_frame(frame) → HashMap<u32, HostNode>

# Pathland Opcode Protocol Specification

**Wire protocol version:** 1
**Status:** Draft
**Format:** Fixed-size (16-byte) opcode engine
**Last Updated:** August 13, 2026

---

## Overview

The Pathland Opcode Protocol is the **fixed-size instruction engine** at the heart of the Rust-first architecture. The **WASM guest engine** emits the application's **declarative view structure** — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing, padding, alignment — as a stream of fixed 16-byte opcodes into a **ring buffer** in **linear memory**. The host renderer consumes the ring and maps the structure onto that platform's **native elements** (GTK4 widgets, DOM elements, HTML).

**The engine does not compute layout and does not emit rects.** Native renderers lay out their own native elements from the constraint properties the engine passes through. This is the Pathland principle: *always render through that platform's native elements.*

This specification supersedes the historical variable-length binary instruction format (which has been removed from the repository).

### Goals

- **Sub-millisecond execution**: every opcode is a fixed 16 bytes; emission is a diff over the retained tree with **zero dynamic heap allocations** in the steady state.
- **L1 CPU cache alignment**: a 64-byte cache line holds exactly **4 opcodes**. Ring slots are 16-byte aligned and densely packed.
- **Reactive emission**: only the nodes that changed emit opcodes. An unchanged tree emits **zero** opcodes (see [Reactive Emission](#reactive-emission)).
- **Linear, deterministic decoding**: the host walks the ring with a single cursor.

### Core Principles

1. **Fixed-size instructions**: every opcode is exactly 16 bytes — no length prefixes, no skippable-variable framing.
2. **Declarative, not positioned**: the engine describes *what* the UI is (stacks, text, constraints), never *where* it is. Native elements compute their own positions.
3. **Numeric IDs**: categories, commands, component types, and properties are numeric.
4. **Native elements**: renderers map the opcode stream onto that platform's native elements — never a generic canvas unless a platform has no native equivalent.
5. **Zero-copy**: the ring and arena are plain regions of the same linear memory shared with the host.
6. **Single-producer / single-consumer**: the guest engine produces; the host renderer consumes. No locks required.

---

## Opcode Format

Every opcode is exactly **16 bytes**:

```
[Category: u8][Command: u8][Flags: u16][A: u32][B: u32][C: u32]
```

| Field | Size | Offset | Description |
|-------|------|--------|-------------|
| `Category` | 1B | 0 | Opcode category (see [Category Table](#category-table)) |
| `Command` | 1B | 1 | Command within the category (see [Command Tables](#command-tables)) |
| `Flags` | 2B | 2 | Category/command-specific flags |
| `A` | 4B | 4 | Primary payload |
| `B` | 4B | 8 | Secondary payload |
| `C` | 4B | 12 | Tertiary payload |

All multi-byte values are **little-endian**. The Rust reference type is `#[repr(C, packed)]`:

```rust
#[repr(C, packed)]
pub struct Opcode {
    pub category: u8,
    pub command: u8,
    pub flags: u16,
    pub a: u32,
    pub b: u32,
    pub c: u32,
}
```

`size_of::<Opcode>() == 16`.

### Payload encoding conventions

- **Float payloads** (`spacing`, `padding`, sizes) are stored as raw `f32` (IEEE 754) bit patterns in a `u32` field.
- **Node IDs** are `u32`.
- **Component types / property IDs** are `u16`; when packed into a 4-byte payload they occupy the low two bytes (the high bytes are reserved / zero unless documented).
- **Arena references** are a `u32` byte offset into the arena region (see [Arena](#arena)).
- **Colors** are packed `0xAARRGGBB` in sRGB (see [Colors](#colors)).

### Reserved ranges

- `Category == 0` is reserved (invalid).
- `Command == 0` in any category is reserved (invalid).
- `Category 0x80-0xFF`: custom/extended categories.

---

## Category Table

| Category | Value | Name | Producer | Description |
|----------|-------|------|----------|-------------|
| `TREE` | `0x01` | Tree mutations | Guest engine | Node create/delete/insert/remove/move |
| `STYLE` | `0x02` | Constraints & tokens | Guest engine | Property values (spacing, padding, …), design tokens |
| `EVENT` | `0x03` | Raw inputs | Host renderer | Pointer down/move/up, key down/up |
| `META` | `0x04` | Control | Both | Reset, environment |

---

## Command Tables

### TREE (0x01)

| Command | Value | A | B | C | Flags | Description |
|---------|-------|---|---|---|-------|-------------|
| `CREATE_NODE` | `0x01` | nodeId | componentType (u16, low) | 0 | — | Create a node of `componentType` |
| `DELETE_NODE` | `0x02` | nodeId | 0 | 0 | — | Delete a node and its subtree |
| `INSERT_CHILD` | `0x03` | parentId | childId | index | `0x0001` = append | Insert `childId` into `parentId` at `index` |
| `REMOVE_CHILD` | `0x04` | parentId | childId | 0 | — | Remove `childId` from `parentId` |
| `MOVE_CHILD` | `0x05` | parentId | childId | newIndex | `0x0001` = append | Move child to `newIndex` (after removal) |

### STYLE (0x02)

The engine does not emit positions. `STYLE` carries the **constraint properties**
that native renderers feed to their own layout — spacing, padding, alignment,
FILL/HUG size hints, colors, fonts.

| Command | Value | A | B | C | Flags | Description |
|---------|-------|---|---|---|-------|-------------|
| `SET_PROPERTY` | `0x01` | nodeId | propertyId (u16, low) + valueType (u8, high byte) | value | — | Set a constraint/style property; `value` depends on `valueType` |
| `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` | `0x02` | arenaRef (path) | valueType (u8) | value | — | Override a design token; path is an arena string |
| `SET_TEXT` | `0x03` | nodeId | arenaRef (utf8) | 0 | — | Set a node's text content |

`SET_PROPERTY` encodes the value type in the **high byte of `B`** (bits 24–31) and the property id in the low two bytes:

```
B = (valueType << 16) | propertyId
```

#### Value types

| Value Type | Value | C / value encoding |
|------------|-------|--------------------|
| `U8` | `0x01` | low byte of C |

278: Tokens are identified by **dot-separated string paths** (e.g. `color.primary`, `space.2`, `font.body`), case-sensitive, lowercase recommended. The `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type (`0x08`) references a token path stored in the arena; `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides a token's value globally.
279: 
280: ### Token Resolution Algorithm
281: 
282: ```
283: FUNCTION resolveToken(tokenPath: string) -> PropertyValue:
284:     IF applicationOverrides.has(tokenPath):
285:         RETURN applicationOverrides[tokenPath]
286:     ELSE IF rendererDefaults.has(tokenPath):
287:         RETURN rendererDefaults[tokenPath]
288:     ELSE IF hasParentToken(tokenPath):
289:         RETURN resolveToken(getParentPath(tokenPath))
290:     ELSE:
291:         RETURN getFallbackValue(tokenPath)
292: ```
293: 
294: ### Renderer Responsibilities
295: 
296: The renderer MUST:
297: 
298: 1. Provide platform-appropriate defaults for all standard tokens (e.g. `color.primary`, `font.body.size`, `space.md`).
299: 2. Accept `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` commands and store overrides.
300: 3. Resolve design-token references in properties.
301: 4. Fall back to defaults when no override exists.
302: 5. Never transmit visual styling rules in the protocol.
303: 
304: The application MAY override any token via `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` and reference tokens via the `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type; it MUST NOT assume specific default token values.
305: 
306: ### Standard Token Catalog
307: 
308: Required core tokens (renderer MUST support with platform-appropriate defaults): `color.primary`, `color.secondary`, `color.background`, `color.surface`, `color.text.primary`, `color.text.secondary`, `color.border`, `font.body.size`, `font.body.weight`, `font.body.family`, `space.xs`–`space.lg`.
309: 
310: Recommended extended tokens: `color.success`, `color.warning`, `color.danger`, `color.info`, `font.heading.1`–`font.heading.6`, `font.size.heading.1`–`6`, `radius.sm`/`md`, `elevation.low`/`high`, `opacity.disabled`.
311: 
312: ---
313: 
314: ## Frame Lifecycle
315: 
316: A frame is a batch of delta opcodes produced by one `emit` pass:
317: 
318: 1. Guest begins a frame.
319: 2. Guest emits the delta opcodes (tree structure and/or property changes) into consecutive ring slots.
320: 3. Guest allocates strings in the arena as needed.
321: 4. Guest `end_frame()`: publishes `writeCursor`, then increments `frameCount`.
322: 5. Host observes `frameCount` change, drains `[readCursor, writeCursor)`, advances `readCursor`.
323: 
324: Because the ring and arena are plain memory, the guest publishes via a single release store of `frameCount`; the host acquires on read.
325: 
326: ---
327: 
328: ## Transport
329: 
330: The opcode protocol is transport-agnostic. Two peer backends carry frames from
331: producer (guest engine) to consumer (host renderer):
332: 
333: | Backend | Scenario | Mechanism |
334: |---------|----------|-----------|
335: | Shared memory | Desktop / native (guest + host share linear memory) | The ring buffer + arena above; zero-copy |
336: | Network batch | SSR → browser (guest and host do **not** share memory) | Serialized batches of opcodes + arena delta |
337: 
338: The `Frame` type is the **transport seam**: a consumer (renderer) applies a
339: frame the same way whether it came from the shared-memory ring or a decoded
340: network batch.
341: 
342: ### Network batch format
343: 
344: ```
345: [u32 magic "PLPL"] [u16 version] [u16 flags] [u32 frameCount] [u32 opcodeCount]
346: [opcode × opcodeCount (16 B each)]
347: [u32 arenaDeltaLen] [arena delta bytes]
348: ```
349: 
350: - **magic / version**: `0x504C504C` (`PLPL`, little-endian on the wire) / `1`.
351:   A decoder MUST reject batches with a mismatched magic or version.
352: - **flags**: direction. `0x0000` = guest → host (tree/style). Bit `0x0001` is
353:   reserved for host → guest (raw-input events), not yet implemented.
354: - **frameCount**: the guest frame counter of the batch's first frame (opcodes
355:   from multiple frames may coalesce into one batch; they remain in order).
356: - **arena delta**: the bytes appended to the bump arena since the previous
357:   batch. The consumer keeps a **mirrored arena** and appends each delta, so
358:   absolute `arenaRef` offsets stay valid — identical to shared memory.
359: - **META::RESET**: a batch containing a reset opcode clears the consumer's
360:   mirrored arena before appending (offsets restart at 0).
361: 
362: ### Batching policy
363: 
364: The producer buffers opcodes and flushes a batch when **either** threshold is
365: reached (first trigger wins):
366: 
367: - **Time**: the interval since the first buffered opcode elapses (default **4 ms**).
368: - **Size**: the accumulated batch reaches a network-frame size (default **1400 bytes**).
369:

371: first frame after connection).

---

## Design Token System

### Core Principle

> **The renderer owns the defaults. The application owns the overrides.**

This ensures a native look-and-feel by default and cross-platform consistency when the application overrides tokens.

### Responsibilities

| Aspect | Owner | Responsibility |
|--------|-------|----------------|
| **Default Token Values** | Renderer | Define platform-appropriate defaults for all standard tokens |
| **Token Overrides** | Application | Specify overrides for cross-platform consistency |
| **Token Resolution** | Renderer | Resolve final token values (override or default) |
| **Platform Adaptation** | Renderer | Adapt default token values to platform conventions |

### Token Identification

Tokens are identified by **dot-separated string paths** (e.g. `color.primary`, `space.2`, `font.body`), case-sensitive, lowercase recommended. The `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type (`0x08`) references a token path stored in the arena; `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides a token's value globally.

### Token Resolution Algorithm

```
FUNCTION resolveToken(tokenPath: string) -> PropertyValue:
    IF applicationOverrides.has(tokenPath):
        RETURN applicationOverrides[tokenPath]
    ELSE IF rendererDefaults.has(tokenPath):
        RETURN rendererDefaults[tokenPath]
    ELSE IF hasParentToken(tokenPath):
        RETURN resolveToken(getParentPath(tokenPath))
    ELSE:
        RETURN getFallbackValue(tokenPath)
```

### Renderer Responsibilities

The renderer MUST:

1. Provide platform-appropriate defaults for all standard tokens (e.g. `color.primary`, `font.body.size`, `space.md`).
2. Accept `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` commands and store overrides.
3. Resolve design-token references in properties.
4. Fall back to defaults when no override exists.
5. Never transmit visual styling rules in the protocol.

The application MAY override any token via `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` and reference tokens via the `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type; it MUST NOT assume specific default token values.

### Standard Token Catalog

Required core tokens (renderer MUST support with platform-appropriate defaults): `color.primary`, `color.secondary`, `color.background`, `color.surface`, `color.text.primary`, `color.text.secondary`, `color.border`, `font.body.size`, `font.body.weight`, `font.body.family`, `space.xs`–`space.lg`.

Recommended extended tokens: `color.success`, `color.warning`, `color.danger`, `color.info`, `font.heading.1`–`font.heading.6`, `font.size.heading.1`–`6`, `radius.sm`/`md`, `elevation.low`/`high`, `opacity.disabled`.

---

## Frame Lifecycle

A frame is a batch of delta opcodes produced by one `emit` pass:

1. Guest begins a frame.
2. Guest emits the delta opcodes (tree structure and/or property changes) into consecutive ring slots.
3. Guest allocates strings in the arena as needed.
4. Guest `end_frame()`: publishes `writeCursor`, then increments `frameCount`.
5. Host observes `frameCount` change, drains `[readCursor, writeCursor)`, advances `readCursor`.

Because the ring and arena are plain memory, the guest publishes via a single release store of `frameCount`; the host acquires on read.

---

## Transport

The opcode protocol is transport-agnostic. Two peer backends carry frames from
producer (guest engine) to consumer (host renderer):

| Backend | Scenario | Mechanism |
|---------|----------|-----------|
| Shared memory | Desktop / native (guest + host share linear memory) | The ring buffer + arena above; zero-copy |
| Network batch | SSR → browser (guest and host do **not** share memory) | Serialized batches of opcodes + arena delta |

The `Frame` type is the **transport seam**: a consumer (renderer) applies a
frame the same way whether it came from the shared-memory ring or a decoded
network batch.

### Network batch format

```
[u32 magic "PLPL"] [u16 version] [u16 flags] [u32 frameCount] [u32 opcodeCount]
[opcode × opcodeCount (16 B each)]
[u32 arenaDeltaLen] [arena delta bytes]
```

- **magic / version**: `0x504C504C` (`PLPL`, little-endian on the wire) / `1`.
  A decoder MUST reject batches with a mismatched magic or version.
- **flags**: direction. `0x0000` = guest → host (tree/style). Bit `0x0001` is
  reserved for host → guest (raw-input events), not yet implemented.
- **frameCount**: the guest frame counter of the batch's first frame (opcodes
  from multiple frames may coalesce into one batch; they remain in order).
- **arena delta**: the bytes appended to the bump arena since the previous
  batch. The consumer keeps a **mirrored arena** and appends each delta, so
  absolute `arenaRef` offsets stay valid — identical to shared memory.
- **META::RESET**: a batch containing a reset opcode clears the consumer's
  mirrored arena before appending (offsets restart at 0).

### Batching policy

The producer buffers opcodes and flushes a batch when **either** threshold is
reached (first trigger wins):

- **Time**: the interval since the first buffered opcode elapses (default **4 ms**).
- **Size**: the accumulated batch reaches a network-frame size (default **1400 bytes**).

Both thresholds are configurable; a producer MAY flush eagerly (e.g. on the
first frame after connection).

---

I now have a complete and thorough understanding of the entire codebase, spec, and current architecture. I have everything I need to write a comprehensive architecture investigation and proposal. This is a large deliverable covering 18 sections.

Let me note the key findings that will shape the proposal:

1. **Retained tree**: exists (Node/Component in pathland-view; flat map in guest).
2. **Views/modifiers**: View/ViewModifier/Modified in pathland-view.
3. **State/dependency tracking**: **DOES NOT EXIST** — this is the biggest gap. No signals, no dependency graph, no dirty tracking. Reconciliation is pure tree-diff.
4. **Reconciliation**: Engine::emit (diff vs snapshot).
5. **Opcodes**: 16-byte fixed-size Opcode exists.
6. **Drivers/renderers**: pathland-host (RenderTree) + GTK demo.
7. **Transport assumption**: The project explicitly built `Frame` as "the transport seam" but there's NO transport trait. The guest currently uses take_batch (network path) even for desktop — the exact problem the user flagged.

Now I'll write the comprehensive architecture proposal. This is a design document, not implementation. I should present it directly as my response since the user asked for a deliverable architecture investigation. I'm in plan mode, so I present the plan/design as text.

Given the scale, I'll produce a well-structured, comprehensive but readable architecture proposal. Let me write it now.

I have completed a thorough investigation of the existing codebase (all crates, the WIT world, the spec, and the GTK demo). Here is the architecture investigation and design proposal.

---

# Pathland Retained-Mode UI Runtime — Architecture Investigation & Proposal

## 0. Executive summary

The existing codebase already implements a solid, well-tested **16-byte fixed-opcode engine**, a **SwiftUI-inspired DSL**, a **diff-based reactive emitter**, a **binary network-batch transport**, and a **GTK4 demo**. It has **four structural gaps** relative to your proposed architecture:

1. **No state/dependency tracking.** There is no signal primitive, no dependency graph, and no dirty-node invalidation. "Reactivity" today is **whole-tree diffing** against a snapshot — the app re-authors the *entire* tree and the engine diffs it. This does not satisfy "only subtrees that depend on changed state are recomputed."
2. **No transport abstraction.** `Frame` is a convenient *type* ("transport seam") but there is **no trait/interface** separating producer→transport→consumer. More importantly, the **GTK desktop demo currently uses the network-batch path** (`take_batch` → `BatchDecoder`), not the shared-memory ring — exactly the misuse you flagged.
3. **No remote/reconnect/resync model.** No sequence numbers, no snapshot/bootstrap protocol, no ack/retransmit.
4. **The retained tree is re-materialized every frame** in both the native and WASM paths (there is no persistent structural identity separate from rebuilding).

Everything else — the opcode format, the ring, the arena, batching, `Frame`, `RenderTree::apply_frame` — is reusable.

I recommend a bounded, well-separated set of new components rather than a rewrite. The core principle throughout: **UI semantics ≠ retained tree ≠ opcode model ≠ transport ≠ driver**, each with an explicit boundary.

---

## 1. Current architecture analysis

### 1.1 Where things live today

| Concern | Location | What exists |
|---|---|---|
| Retained tree | `pathland-view` `Node` + `Component`; `pathland-guest` `FlatNode` map | Value tree (`Vec<Node>`) / flat id map |
| Views / modifiers | `pathland-view` `View`, `ViewModifier`, `Modified<V,M>`, macros | Rust DSL; modifiers mutate a node's properties (no wrapper nodes) |
| State + dependency tracking | **None anywhere** | Missing entirely — the central gap |
| Reconciliation | `pathland-engine` `Engine::emit` | Whole-tree diff vs `SnapshotNode` slab + gen-stamps; zero-alloc steady state |
| Opcode model | `pathland-opcode` `Opcode` | 16-byte `[Cat|Cmd|Flags|A|B|C]`, LE, v1 |
| Transport | `pathland-opcode` `Guest`/`Host` (ring) + `pathland-transport` (`BatchEncoder`/`Decoder`) | Two concrete backends, **no trait** |
| Driver / renderer | `pathland-host` `RenderTree` + `pathland-gtk-demo` | `apply_frame(&Frame)` → native-element desc → GTK widgets |

### 1.2 The critical current assumption (Problem you flagged)

The demo's data flow is:
```
DSL build_tree → assign_ids → import_tree (WIT builder calls) → guest.emit
   → take_batch() → [bytes across WIT ABI] → BatchDecoder → RenderTree → GTK
```
- The ring/arena live **only inside the guest's WASM linear memory** (`State.mem`).
- The host **never reads the guest's ring directly**; it copies bytes out via `take_batch` and re-decodes them with `BatchDecoder` (a network path).
- This is because the WASM component model isolates guest memory — the host cannot get a raw memory handle through `bindgen!`.

**This is the root architectural mistake to fix.** The desktop path must be: producer writes to a **shared ring that the consumer reads in place** — no batch, no copy. The network path uses batch + WebSocket.

### 1.3 What's reusable vs. what must change

**Reusable as-is:**
- The 16-byte `Opcode` format + constants (stable, conformant).
- `pathland-opcode` `Guest`/`Host` + ring + arena (the shared-memory transport machinery).
- `Frame` as the *unit* of consumption (a driver consumes a `Frame`).
- `pathland-transport` `BatchEncoder`/`BatchDecoder`/`BatchPolicy`/`Batcher` (the network path).
- `pathland-view` DSL for authoring and `assign_ids` for identity.
- `pathland-host` `RenderTree::apply_frame` (renderer-neutral decode).
- The WIT world (`pathland.wit`) as the language-agnostic surface.

**Must change / add:**
- **A `Transport` abstraction trait** with producers/consumers on both ends, so the runtime never hardcodes ring-vs-batch.
- **A shared-memory bridge for the WASM/desktop case** so the host can consume the ring in place (or, if WASM isolation prevents it, a clear defined bridge — see §7 and risks).
- **A state/dependency-tracking layer** (signals + dep graph + dirty set) feeding *incremental* recomputation, replacing whole-tree re-authoring.
- **A view identity/reuse layer** so subtrees aren't rebuilt wholesale (needed to make fine-grained invalidation meaningful).
- **A snapshot/transport-envelope channel** for SSR connect/reconnect/resync.
- **An explicit `Driver` consumer abstraction** in the host layer.

---

## 2. Proposed component diagram

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        UI Runtime                             │
│                                                              │
│  ┌───────────┐   ┌──────────────────┐   ┌─────────────────┐  │
│  │  State    │──▶│ Dependency Graph │──▶│  Dirty Subtree  │  │
│  │ (signals) │   │ (state→view edges)│   │ (recompute set) │  │
│  └───────────┘   └──────────────────┘   └────────┬────────┘  │
│                                                   ▼           │
│  ┌───────────────┐   ┌────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  View DSL     │──▶│  Retained Tree + View Identity      │  │
│  │ (pathland-    │   │  + Incremental Recomputation         │  │
│  │  view)        │   └───────────────────┬────────────────┘  │
│  └───────────────┘                       ▼                   │
│  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Opcode Engine  │──▶│  OpcodeStream (Frame producer)   │  │
│  └─────────────────┘   └──────────────────────────────────┘  │
└───────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────┘
                                            │ OpcodeStream / Frame
                                             ▼
                                ┌───────────────────────┐
                                │   Transport trait     │
                                │  (batch = unit of xfer)│
                                └───────┬──────┬─────────┘
                                        ▼      ▼
                            ┌────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐
                            │ RingTransport  │ │ NetBatchTransport│
                            │ (shared mem,   │ │ (batch + WS/IPC) │
                            │  SPSC, zero-   │ └────────┬─────────┘
                            │  copy in place)│          ▼
                            └───────┬────────┘    WebSocket/IPC
                                    ▼                 ▼
                            ┌────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐
                            │ DriverConsumer │ │ RemoteDecoder    │
                            │ (native GTK/   │ │ → DriverConsumer │
                            │  AppKit/...)   │ └──────────────────┘
                            └───────┬────────┘
                                    ▼
                            ┌────────────────┐
                            │ RenderTree /   │
                            │ native widgets │
                            └────────────────┘
```

**Boundary rule (the five separations):**
- **UI semantics** (state, reactivity intent) → lives in the runtime app layer, never serialized.
- **Retained tree** (what the UI structurally *is*) → `pathland-view`/engine; the source of truth for emission.
- **Opcode model** (binary protocol) → `pathland-opcode`; the only thing that crosses a transport.
- **Transport** (how a batch moves) → `pathland-transport`; an injected dependency, invisible to the runtime.
- **Driver** (how a stream becomes native UI) → host layer; consumes `Frame`s, never sees a transport.

---

## 3. Proposed Rust traits / interfaces

### 3.1 Transport abstraction

I evaluated `trait OpcodeTransport { fn submit(&mut self, batch: &OpcodeBatch); }` and a peer-to-peer alternative. `submit(batch)` is insufficient: you also need the **reverse direction** (host→guest events over the same transport) and a way to model the two ends. I propose a **bidirectional, two-ended transport abstraction** where each end is opened independently — this keeps local (same-process) and remote (async) transports on equal footing:

```rust
// A transport carries opcode Frames in both directions.
// Local transports may be zero-copy; remote transports serialize.

pub trait GuestTransport {                       // producer side (engine → driver)
    /// Deliver a frame to the consumer. `flush` signals "render now".
    fn send_frame(&mut self, frame: &Frame<'_>, flush: bool) -> Result<(), TransportError>;
    /// Register a receiver for host → guest inputs (events).
    fn set_input_sink(&mut self, sink: Box<dyn InputSink>);
}

pub trait DriverTransport {                      // consumer side (driver reads)
    /// Blocking or non-blocking next frame.
    fn poll(&mut self) -> Result<Option<FrameBatch<'_>>, TransportError>;
    fn send_input(&mut self, ev: &Event) -> Result<(), TransportError>; // host → guest
}

pub trait InputSink { fn dispatch(&mut self, ev: &Event); }
```

**Why two traits instead of one:** the producer and consumer are often different sides of a process/IPC boundary. A single `submit` trait can't express "consumer pulls" vs "producer pushes", backpressure, or the reverse event channel cleanly. The `Frame` (not raw opcodes, not an internal enum) is the unit — reuse `pathland_opcode::Frame`.

**Backpressure model:** `send_frame` returns `TransportError::Backpressure` when the consumer hasn't drained (ring full / socket buffer full). The runtime treats it as "retain frame, retry later" — the retained tree is already the source of truth, so nothing is lost.

### 3.2 Driver/consumer abstraction

Evaluate `Transport → Driver` vs `Transport → OpcodeConsumer → Driver`. I recommend **`Transport → OpcodeConsumer → Driver`** for the host layer:

```rust
pub trait OpcodeConsumer {                       // renderer-neutral
    fn apply(&mut self, frame: &Frame<'_>) -> Result<(), ApplyError>;
}

pub trait Driver {                               // renderer-specific (GTK/AppKit)
    fn apply(&mut self, frame: &Frame<'_>) -> Result<(), DriverError>;
    fn target_at(&self, x: f32, y: f32) -> Option<u32>; // hit-test -> node id (for events)
}
```

The consumer (`RenderTree`) is renderer-neutral; the `Driver` maps `RenderTree`/opcodes to native widgets. A ring transport and a WebSocket decoder both produce `Frame`s that feed the **same** `Driver` after `OpcodeConsumer`. This keeps "driver consumes opcodes regardless of how they arrived."

---

## 4. Proposed opcode model

**The current model is already excellent and stable — keep it.** Evaluate each factor you listed:

| Factor | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Fixed vs variable | **Fixed 16 bytes** — keep. Cache-line aligned (4/line), no length prefixes, linear decode. |
| Header | Category(1)+Command(1)+Flags(2) = 4-byte header inside the 16-byte opcode — keep. |
| Payload encoding | A/B/C (3×u32). LE. Float via bit patterns. Numeric ids. Keep. |
| Node/view IDs | u32 node ids. Stable ids = contract. **Keep; formalize id stability as a first-class invariant.** |
| Property IDs | u16 packed into `B` low half + valueType high byte. Keep. |
| String/data handling | Bump **arena** with `[u32 len][bytes]`, arenaRef offset. Keep — this is what decouples strings from opcode size. |
| Alignment | 16-byte opcodes, 64-B cache line = 4 opcodes. Ring base 16-byte aligned. Keep. |
| Endianness | Little-endian everywhere. Keep. |
| Versioning | `version=1` in header/Arena. Keep; bump on breaking change. |
| Fwd/bwd compat | Category `0x80-0xFF` reserved for custom extensions; unknown commands decodable (skip-able) — **formalize** "unknown opcode must be skipped, not fatal." |
| Batching | Multiple frames coalesce; arena-delta. Keep. |
| Frame boundaries | `frameCount` watermark. Keep. |
| Error handling | RingError/BatchError. Keep; add transport-level errors. |
| Self-contained vs side tables | Opcodes reference arena (side table). Keep — this is the right call; a fully self-contained stream would bloat strings into every opcode. |

**One recommended addition for the remote/reconnect story (see §5): a `SNAPSHOT` / bootstrap command** in `META` (e.g. `META:SNAPSHOT_BEGIN/END` or a dedicated `SNAPSHOT` opcode) that signals "the following Frames rebuild the full retained tree from scratch." This is *renderer-neutral* (you're reconstructing the tree, not sending glyphs), fits declarative semantics.

**Wire independence:** The spec already correctly avoids `bincode`-style Rust struct serialization — opcodes are byte-explicit. This is a pre-existing strength; preserve it and **never** couple the wire to a Rust `#[derive(Serialize)]`.

---

## 5. Proposed OpcodeBatch model

The unit that crosses a transport should be a **Frame batch**, distinct from the raw opcode stream, because a batch may consolidate several Frames and must carry transport metadata. Introduce (in `pathland-transport`):

```rust
pub struct OpcodeBatch<'a> {
    pub frames: Vec<Frame<'a>>,      // or a streaming view when zero-copy
    pub frame_count: u32,            // last frame covered
    pub needs_render: bool,          // "flush now" hint (cursor/pointer committed)
}
```

Keep the existing wire-batch format for **serialized** transports (the byte layout you already specify: `magic|version|flags|frameCount|opcodeCount|opcodes|arenaDeltaLen|arenaDelta`). The `OpcodeBatch` type is the **in-memory** abstraction a transport impl either (a) writes into a ring (zero-copy) or (b) serializes into bytes. **Do not conflate the in-memory batch type with the wire format** — the wire format stays a spec; the in-memory type is an implementation detail of a transport impl.

---

## 6. Proposed transport abstraction

Final recommendation (see §3.1 for the traits). Concretely, implement two transports behind the same interface:

- **`RingTransport`** — wraps `pathland-opcode` `Guest`/`Host` over a shared `Vec<u8>` (linear memory). Producer side = `Guest`; consumer side = `Host` → `Frame`. Zero-copy, SPSC, lock-free.
- **`WebSocketTransport` / `NetBatchTransport`** — producer side = `Batcher` (time/size) → serialized bytes → socket; consumer side = `BatchDecoder` → `Frame`.

**Separation of concerns — where batching lives (§6 of your questions):** I evaluated A (`Engine→OpcodeBatch→Transport`), B (`Engine→Stream→Transport batches`), C (`Engine→frame→Transport`). Recommendation: **C as the semantic boundary + A as the transport-delegated batching.**

- The **runtime/engine produces `Frame`s** (one per emission) and knows **nothing** about batching policy. This is option C — it preserves the semantics: the engine emits what changed, period.
- The **transport** (specifically its producer side / encoder) decides **when and how to group** consecutive Frames — into a ring (each Frame = contiguous slots) or into a network batch on a time/size policy (option A). Batching policy is a **transport concern**, never a runtime concern.

This is the key clean separation: the UI runtime produces incremental updates without knowing whether the consumer is local GTK (immediate) or a remote browser (coalesced/serialized).

---

## 7. Ring-buffer transport design (the desktop path — fix the misuse)

The goal: **native driver reads opcodes directly from shared memory, minimal overhead.**

**Current state:** `pathland-opcode` already has `Guest` (producer: writes at `writeCursor`, bumps `frameCount`) and `Host` (consumer: reads `[readCursor, writeCursor)`, advances). This is a correct SPSC ring with release/acquire semantics (`frameCount` as the publication watermark). **Reuse it.**

**The problem to solve for desktop+WASM:** in the WASM/wasmtime model, the ring lives in the guest's isolated linear memory and `bindgen!` won't hand the host a raw memory handle. Options:

- **(A) Guest exports a `peek-arena` + the host owns memory (recommended for WASM):** The **host allocates the shared linear memory buffer** and passes it into the guest (imported memory), OR the guest exposes the ring region via a WIT function. Since raw memory can't cross the canonical ABI, the practical WASM pattern is: **guest writes opcodes; host pulls via a WIT `read-ring()` that returns the *new* opcodes + arena delta as bytes.** That is functionally the *batch* path again, but we can name it explicitly as the "shared-memory bridge" and, importantly, **make the driver consume it via `Host`/`Frame` identical to native** — so the driver code path is shared even if the WASM transport must copy across the ABI.
- **(B) Native embed (no WASM) for desktop:** guest + host are the same native process sharing one `Vec<u8>`; the ring is genuinely zero-copy. This is the true SPSC shared ring your spec describes. It **does not** exercise the WASM/WIT bridge for desktop.

**Recommendation:** Keep the WIT foundation as the canonical engine surface (you need this for cross-language). For the **desktop GTK demo**, the *renderer* must consume a ring. Two coherent sub-options:
1. **Native ring transport**: the host embeds the engine natively (shared `Vec`), uses `Host` directly → true zero-copy shared ring; the same `pathland-view`/engine crates are reused (not a divergent copy). The WIT component remains canonical for *other language* hosts.
2. **WASM ring bridge**: host feeds guest memory and pulls `Frame`s; "shared memory" is honored at the `Frame`/`RenderTree` layer even though bytes cross the ABI.

I need your decision here — see Open Questions.

**Ring design specifics to honor and extend:**
- SPSC, power-of-two slot count, mask wrap. Keep.
- `frameCount` release/acquire watermark. Keep.
- **Cache-line contention:** producer cursor and consumer cursor should live in **separate cache lines** (pad header fields) to avoid false sharing. Current header packs them together (offsets `0x1C`/`0x20`). **Recommend separating** head/tail into distinct cache lines when we formalize the ring as a first-class type.
- **Variable-sized opcodes:** you asked. Keep **fixed 16-byte** opcodes and put variable data in the arena. Do not make opcodes variable-sized — it destroys the L1 alignment and linear-decode property.
- **Batch boundaries in the ring:** each emission = a contiguous slice of slots delimited by `begin_frame`/`end_frame` (already modeled via `frame_start`). Keep: the consumer drains a complete frame.
- **Overflow/full:** producer must not overwrite unconsumed slots → `RingError::Full` → backpressure. Keep; route to `TransportError::Backpressure`.
- **Wakeup/notification:** for a PAINT consumer, the producer should signal "a frame is ready" — on desktop this is often "queue a main-loop redraw" (glib idle/timeout) rather than a condvar. Make the notification a **callback/config**, not baked in.
- **Consume-without-copy:** driver reads `&[u8]` slots directly (already the case via `Frame`). Keep zero-copy on the read side.

**Arena in the ring transport:** since the arena is *shared memory* in the native case, the consumer reads strings via `frame.arena_str` directly — no delta needed. The arena-delta machinery is **only** for serialized (network) transports. Keep them separate — do not couple ring reads to delta-mirroring.

---

## 8. WebSocket transport design

Preserve exact opcode semantics; add a thin **envelope** around batches:

```
TransportFrame {
    protocol_version: u16
    sequence_number:  u32   // monotonic, for ordering + resync
    message_type:     u8    // SNAPSHOT | INCREMENTAL | ACK | RESYNC_REQ
    flags:            u8
    opcode_count:     u32
    payload:          [opcode batch bytes]  // the existing batch format, or a snapshot
}
```

**Why a separate envelope is useful**: it carries sequence numbers and message type *independent of the opcode grammar*, so a decoder can detect a `SNAPSHOT` vs an `INCREMENTAL` and re-sync without parsing opcodes. The opcode binary representation inside is preserved exactly (don't invent a second opcode encoding).

**Server side:**
```
generate opcodes → (batcher, time/size) → wrap batch in TransportFrame(seq=N) → send on WS
```
**Client side:**
```
recv → validate magic/version → unwrap envelope → BatchDecoder → Frame → Driver
```

**Acks:** client sends `ACK(seq)` periodically (or NACK on gap). The server can use acks to trim its outbound buffer and to trigger `RESYNC` on gap. Over WebSocket with reliable delivery, acks are mostly informational; they matter for QUIC/IPC without reliability.

---

## 9. Remote rendering lifecycle (connect after UI exists)

The critical problem you raised: **a client connecting after the server already built a UI.** The fix is a snapshot/bootstrap protocol, not just incremental deltas:

**Lifecycle:**
1. Client connects → sends `RESYNC_REQ` (or `HELLO` with its `protocol_version`).
2. Server checks version compatibility → if OK, sends a **`SNAPSHOT` message**: a full retained-tree reconstruction (either a fresh full render from the engine, or a re-emit producing create/insert/set for every node — the engine's existing full first-emit already produces exactly this).
3. Server then streams `INCREMENTAL` messages and *continues* from the sequence number at connection time; concurrent changes are safe because a snapshot is atomic at the server (single producer).
4. Client applies SNAPSHOT to clear + rebuild `RenderTree`, then applies INCREMENTALs in seq order.

**Sequence numbers & reconnect:**
- Monotonic `sequence_number` per message.
- Client tracks last-applied seq; on reconnect it sends `RESYNC_REQ(last_seq)`.
- Server either replays buffered INCREMENTALs after `last_seq` (if still in its buffer) **or** sends a fresh SNAPSHOT (if the buffer ran out). **Snapshot on reconnect is the robust default** — it's simpler and correct; replay-with-buffer is an optimization.
- **Version compatibility:** server rejects clients with unsupported `protocol_version` (or upgrades the stream). Define a compatibility policy (same major = OK).

**Lost batches:** with buffered replay + acks, the server can retransmit; with SNAPSHOT-resync, losses self-heal. Both use the same `TransportFrame` machinery.

---

## 10. Driver / consumer design

- **`OpcodeConsumer` (renderer-neutral):** `RenderTree` (already exists) applies `Frame` deltas. This is what both native and remote drivers share.
- **`Driver` (renderer-specific):** GTK today; later AppKit/UIKit/LVGL. Maps `RenderTree` → native widgets, and does **hit-testing** (`target_at(x,y) → node id`) to resolve raw inputs to node ids (the renderer's own output cache — allowed by statelessness; not app state).

**Recommended model:** `Transport → OpcodeConsumer → Driver`. The transport (even the WASM bridge) produces `Frame`s; the consumer builds the native-element description; the driver renders. Both `RingTransport` and `WebSocketTransport` terminate in the **same** `Driver` after `BatchDecoder`/`Host` — this is exactly the property you want.

---

## 11. Reconnection / resynchronization strategy

(Consolidating §9) — implement:
- `TransportFrame.sequence_number` for ordering and gap detection.
- `message_type = SNAPSHOT | INCREMENTAL | ACK | RESYNC_REQ`.
- Ack-based window + server outbound buffer (bounded).
- On any gap or reconnect → **SNAPSHOT resync** (correct default), with buffered-replay as an optional fast path.
- Client-side: on `SNAPSHOT`, clear `RenderTree` and rebuild; apply INCREMENTALs in order; track last-applied seq.
- Version gate on `protocol_version`.

---

## 12. WASM / browser strategy

Let me address your specific points:

- **SharedArrayBuffer + Web Workers:** A browser worker can host the engine and share `SharedArrayBuffer` with the main thread; the main-thread driver reads the ring with atomics — this is the browser analogue of the native shared ring, and can reuse the **same `Frame`/`RenderTree`/`Driver`** semantics.
- **Browser main-thread restrictions:** DOM is main-thread-only; so the *driver* runs on the main thread, while the *engine* may run on a worker or the server. This is naturally expressed by our separation (engine/transport vs driver).
- **WASM ↔ JS boundary:** bytes must cross JS↔WASM; `take-batch`/decoder is acceptable, but if you want zero-copy in-browser, use `SharedArrayBuffer` + the ring (engine in a worker). The opcode representation is **identical** in WASM (it already runs in WASM today via `pathland-guest`).
- **Browser driver input:** feeds raw `EVENT` opcodes back through `InputSink`/`dispatch` — same path as desktop.
- **Recommendation:** define the browser driver to **consume the same `Frame` stream** regardless of whether it arrived via `SharedArrayBuffer` (worker) or a `WebSocket` (server render). Both decode into the same consumer/driver. This gives "browser uses the same opcode semantics as native."

---

## 13. Performance considerations

**Local/native path (optimized for ~zero overhead):**
```
state change → dirty subtree → recompute → Engine::emit → write to shared ring → Driver poll → render
              (no alloc if possible)   (16-B opcodes, SPSC)   (zero-copy read)
```
- Copies: **0** (native shared ring). Allocations: avoidable in engine (already zero-alloc steady state). Latency: one frame, main-loop immediate.
- **Add `select(...)`/query-based recompute:** the big win is *not* re-authoring the whole tree — only dirty subtrees rebuild. This is where the dependency graph pays off.

**Remote path (accepts serialization/copy):**
```
... → Engine::emit → batcher (time/size) → serialize (opcodes + arena delta) → WS → decode → mirror arena → RenderTree
```
- Copies: engine→batch buffer, batch→socket, socket→client buf. Allocations: batcher buffer. Serialization: header + LE fields only (cheap). Latency: up to batch interval (4 ms) + network RTT.
- **Arena delta** already avoids re-sending unchanged strings.

**Key insight to protect:** the **native path must not route through the batch serializer/deserializer**. Today it does (via `take_batch` → `BatchDecoder`). That adds a serialization + copy + an arena-mirror churn on every frame for a *local* render. Fixing this (shared-ring on native, or an explicit WASM bridge that still avoids batch double-decode) is a measurable win.

---

## 14. Threading / concurrency considerations

- **Engine/producer:** single thread. Retained tree mutated only here → no locks on the tree. This preserves SPSC.
- **Transport:** the producer side is called from the runtime thread; the consumer side from the driver (e.g. GTK main thread) or a socket reader thread.
- **WASM component:** today uses a `Mutex<State>` global (single-threaded per instance); keep single-threaded, drop the mutex for clarity (or keep for safety).
- **Ring:** SPSC lock-free; keep producer/consumer cursors in separate cache lines. No multi-producer/multi-consumer — that's a deliberate scope guardrail.
- **Driver:** native driver on the event-loop thread; must not block on a full ring for more than a frame (use backpressure → "drain on next idle").
- **Network:** socket reader thread → decode → hand `Frame` to main-thread driver via a small channel (or decode on main thread if cheap).

---

## 15. Error handling strategy

Layer errors explicitly:
- **Engine:** `EmitError` (ring full → backpressure). Already `RingError`.
- **Transport:** `TransportError { Backpressure | Closed | Io | Protocol { BadVersion, BadMagic, Truncated, Checksum } }`.
- **Driver:** `DriverError { NotFound, UnsupportedComponent, WidgetError }`.
- **Decode:** `BatchError` (already exists).
- **Policies:** on protocol error → drop connection + optional resync. On unknown opcode → skip (forward/backward compat). On backpressure → retain frame, retry next idle. Rollback of partial frames: a frame is applied atomically by the consumer (drain-complete before apply); if a frame is malformed, discard the rest of that frame.

---

## 16. Versioning strategy

- **Opcode wire version:** bump `version` (currently 1) on any breaking change to opcode layout/semantics. Pre-release changes allowed while version stays 1, per existing policy.
- **Transport batch/envelope version:** separate — can evolve independently of opcode semantics (add features to the envelope without renumbering opcodes). Keep `protocol_version` in `TransportFrame`.
- **Sending:** `SNAPSHOT` carries the engine's retained-tree version; a client mismatch → resync.
- **Forward compat:** skip unknown opcodes/commands; reserve category `0x80-0xFF` for custom extensions.

---

## 17. Migration plan from current code (bounded, not a rewrite)

1. **Define the transport traits + `OpcodeBatch`/`TransportFrame` types** in `pathland-transport` (additive; existing batch format/batcher unchanged).
2. **Add a `RingTransport`** wrapping existing `Guest`/`Host` over a shared `Vec` (native case) — demonstrate true shared-memory consumption.
3. **Fix the GTK demo** to consume via the shared ring (native embed) or an explicit WASM ring *bridge* that feeds `Host`/`Frame` (not batch-decode on desktop). This directly addresses the misuse you flagged.
4. **Add `META:SNAPSHOT` + `TransportFrame` + ack/resync** to the wire spec for the remote path.
5. **Build dependency-tracking + signals (the big-new gap):** add a `signal` primitive + a dependency graph + dirty-subtree recompute **on top of** the existing `Engine::emit` (the engine still does final diff; the new layer makes recompute *incremental* instead of whole-tree). This is the largest piece and should be its own goal.
6. **Add a `Driver` trait + an `OpcodeConsumer`** layer so renderers plug in without touching the runtime.
7. Migrate tests; keep `cargo test` green at each step; the existing 64 tests are the safety net.

---

## 18. Risks and open questions

### Architectural criticisms (challenging the direction)

1. **The "shared ring for desktop + WASM/WIT" requirement is internally tension-ridden.** The WASM component model isolates guest memory; `bindgen!` won't expose a raw memory handle. So "the driver reads the guest's ring in place" is **not directly expressible** through the WIT/wasmtime surface as it stands. You must pick: (a) native embed for desktop (true zero-copy ring, but desktop no longer hosts WASM), or (b) an explicit WASM ring **bridge** (host pulls `Frame`s via WIT — bytes cross the ABI, so not literally shared memory in the copy-free sense, but the driver consumes `Frame`s identically). **Choose deliberately; do not pretend both are literal zero-copy.**
2. **Whole-tree re-authoring vs incremental recompute.** Today, even with a dependency graph, the DSL `build()` rebuilds the entire `Node` tree. To truly recompute *only dirty subtrees*, you need **view identity + subtree reuse** (nodes that didn't change are not rebuilt). That's a significant piece beyond just "signals." The current `assign_ids`-then-rebuild doesn't achieve it. This is the hardest part of the runtime and currently missing.
3. **Dependency granularity.** A dep graph at the *node* level, with per-property edges, is complex. Recommendation: start at **subtree granularity** (a dirty subtree re-emits its own diff), and only later refine to per-property if profiles demand it. Avoid over-engineering initially.
4. **`Frame` as the transport unit vs a proper batch type.** `Frame` conflates "one emission" with "what crosses a transport." Cleaving `OpcodeBatch` (transport unit) from `Frame` (emission unit) is the right separation and avoids leaking emission semantics into transports.
5. **Arena-delta coupling.** The existing arena-delta is a *serialized-transport* mechanism. Do not let it leak into the shared-ring (native) path, where the arena is directly readable. Keeping them separate is both correct and faster.

### Open questions (need your decision)

1. **Desktop transport model** — native embed (true shared ring, WIT stays canonical for other languages) vs WASM ring bridge (host pulls frames via WIT, driver consumes `Frame` but bytes cross ABI)? **This is the crux.**
2. **Dependency granularity** for the first incremental-recompute goal — subtree-level (recommended) or per-property?
3. **Batching** — confirm the transport owns batching (engine emits Frames; transport groups) vs runtime-aware batching.
4. **Reconnect default** — SNAPSHOT-resync on reconnect (recommended, simpler/correct) vs buffered-replay-with-fallback.
5. **Browser** — SharedArrayBuffer+worker (zero-copy) or WebSocket (server-render) as the first browser driver? They need different seeding but share decoder/driver.
6. **Scope/sequence** — should the dependency-tracking + incremental-recompute be a separate tracked goal from the transport cleanup? I recommend splitting them (transport fix is small and urgent; reactivity is large).

---

This is the architecture proposal. It is deliberately a **design/plan document** — I have not written any implementation code, per your instruction to review boundaries first.

I want to confirm the **single most important decision** before any implementation plan is finalized, because it determines the transport architecture for desktop:

Your two requirements are the crux, and they interact in a specific, important way. Let me address them precisely.

## Requirement 1: "Components built in Rust usable in other languages without per-component wrappers"

This is about the **language-agnostic surface** — what Java, Swift, C#, etc. call. Your instinct is right, and it's the **opposite** of exposing `vstack!`/`Text`/`Button` as individual WIT functions per component.

Two distinct facts to separate:

- **WIT does NOT require per-component wrappers.** A WIT world exposes *interfaces* (functions, records, variants). You already expose **one flat `builder` interface** — `create-node(id, variant)`, `insert-child`, `set-property` — where `component` and `property` are **variants**. So Java/Swift/C# get a small, fixed, closed set of bindings generated once (by `wit-bindgen`), and they build any component by calling the same few functions. **No wrapper per component.** This is already true and is the correct design.

- **The trade-off you must accept:** because the `component`/`property` are **variants** (closed, compiled-in), **adding a new component/property requires a WIT change + binding regeneration.** That's the price of "no wrappers per component." The alternative (per-component interfaces) gives you extensibility per component but multiplies bindings. Keep the **flat variant-based world** — it's the right call for "no per-component wrappers."

So requirement 1 is **already satisfied by the current flat WIT world**, and it's compatible with zero-copy desktop — **as long as the transport is separated from the component surface.** The WIT `builder`/`engine`/`input`/`app` interfaces are about *tree semantics*, not about *how bytes move*. Zero-copy transport lives **below** the WIT boundary.

## Requirement 2: "Zero-copy on desktop"

Here is the critical clarification that resolves the apparent conflict:

**Zero-copy transport and the WIT component surface are at DIFFERENT layers.** You do not have to choose between them:

```
[Language surface]   Java / Swift / C#  →  call WIT (flat builder/engine)  →  cross-language ✓
[Transport]         the opcode stream moves somewhere
                       ├─ desktop: shared ring (zero-copy)   ✓
                       └─ remote:   batch + WebSocket (copy)
[Driver]            consumes Frames
```

**The key architectural rule:** the **runtime engine** (which produces opcodes) and the **transport** (which moves them) are two things. For zero-copy *desktop*, the renderer must consume the ring **in the same address space as the producer**. There are exactly two ways to have producer and consumer share one address space:

1. **Native embed** — engine and driver are the same native process (Rust), sharing one `Vec<u8>` ring. Zero-copy, trivially. But then the desktop *driver process* doesn't go through WASM.

2. **Native driver + WASM engine in the SAME process → but the WASM guest's memory is not addressable by the native driver.**

**The honest, hard constraint:** with the engine inside a **WASM/wasmtime component**, the driver cannot zero-copy the ring because wasmtime isolates the guest's linear memory from native code. `bindgen!` doesn't expose a raw pointer to guest RAM, and even at the low level, wasmtime's memory is a wasm-owned region the host shouldn't scribble on directly. So **"WASM engine + zero-copy shared ring to a native driver" is not achievable in wasmtime.**

## Therefore, the architecture that satisfies BOTH of your requirements

Combine them this way:

- **The engine (retained tree + dependency tracking + opcode emission) lives in `pathland-engine` as plain Rust** — this is the single source of truth, compiled once, usable by all languages via the **flat WIT world** (no per-component wrappers). Requirement 1 ✓.

- **Desktop zero-copy:** the **driver and engine share one process address space.** Two concrete shapes:
  - **(a) Native driver, native engine:** GTK driver links `pathland-engine` directly, shares a `Vec<u8>` ring → true zero-copy. The **same** flat WIT world is *still available* and demonstrated for cross-language hosts, but the desktop hot path doesn't route through WASM.
  - **(b) Native driver, WASM engine → zero-copy is NOT possible** in wasmtime.

So the decision narrows to: **for the desktop path, do you need the GTK driver to host the WASM engine, or is it acceptable that the GTK driver is native-Rust (zero-copy) while the WASM component remains the canonical cross-language engine used by Java/Swift/C#/Quarkus?**

Given your two stated requirements, I strongly recommend: **native driver + native engine on desktop (zero-copy), WIT world as the canonical cross-language surface, and the WASM component as the engine for remote/non-Rust hosts.** This is the only configuration in which zero-copy desktop and no-per-component-wrappers both hold simultaneously.

Let me confirm this understanding before finalizing the migration plan:

The flat WIT world + WASM component remain the canonical cross-language engine for Java/Swift/C#/Quarkus/remote. No per-component wrappers. Zero-copy and cross-language both hold.
options.label: Native desktop ring + WIT for other languages (Recommended)

options.description: The GTK driver must host the WASM engine. Accept that zero-copy is NOT possible here (wasmtime isolates guest memory); use the WASM ring bridge which copies across the ABI. Cross-language preserved; desktop is logical rather than physical shared memory.
options.label: GTK hosts WASM engine (no physical zero-copy)

This is the decisive clarification, and it changes the conclusion. Your requirement is now precise:

> "If I write a desktop app in **Swift**, I need to use components written in **Rust** and still have **zero-copy** opcodes."

So the desktop app is **not** a Rust GTK app — it's a **Swift app** (on macOS, so AppKit/SwiftUI), using Rust components, with zero-copy opcodes to a native Swift driver. This is a different and much sharper requirement. Let me reason it through carefully.

## The new, precise requirement

- **Language:** Swift (desktop app).
- **Components:** built in Rust, consumed by Swift **without per-component wrappers**.
- **Opcodes:** must reach the Swift native driver **zero-copy**.

## What this means for the transport layer

The transport boundary is now **Rust → Swift within one macOS process**. The question "zero-copy across a Rust/Swift boundary" depends entirely on **how the Rust code is packaged** for the Swift app:

### Case A: Rust compiled to a native static/dynamic library (cdylib), linked into the Swift app
- Rust and Swift are in the **same process, same address space**.
- The Swift driver and the Rust engine can share a **ring buffer in a `Vec<u8>`/`UnsafeMutableRawPointer` region** that Swift allocates and Rust writes (or vice versa). Swift reads opcodes directly from that buffer via memory pointers → **true zero-copy**.
- **No wrappers per component:** Swift uses the **flat WIT world** (create-node/insert-child/set-property as variants). `wit-bindgen` can generate Swift bindings for the same flat world — a **fixed, closed** set, not per-component. So requirement 1 holds.
- **This is the correct configuration for your requirement.**

### Case B: Rust compiled to WASM, embedded via wasmtime in the Swift app
- wasmtime isolates the guest (Rust-in-WASM) memory from the Swift host.
- Swift driver **cannot** read the ring zero-copy across the wasm boundary.
- So **WASM + zero-copy-to-Swift is impossible** — same conclusion as before, but now calibrated to a Swift host.

## The decisive resolution

Your requirement (Swift desktop + zero-copy) **forces Case A**: the Rust engine is compiled to a **native library** (cdylib, or a Swift Package with a Rust build step) that the Swift app links, sharing an in-process ring. The **WIT world** remains the *interface contract* — `wit-bindgen` generates the Swift bindings for the flat `builder`/`engine`/`input`/`app` world once, with **no per-component wrappers**.

The **WASM component** is then for **remote/other** hosts that genuinely can't link native Rust (e.g., a Java/Quarkus server, a browser) — where zero-copy isn't required and copying across WASM/WebSocket is acceptable.

This is actually a clean, defensible architecture:

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 One desktop app process (Swift)          │
│                                                          │
│  Swift UI code ──calls flat WIT world (wit-bindgen)──►   │
│                                                          │
│  Rust engine (native cdylib, SAME address space)         │
│   retained tree + dependency tracking + opcode emission  │
│              │                                           │
│              ▼  shared ring (Vec/raw mem, zero-copy)     │
│  Swift driver reads opcodes in place → AppKit/...        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Separately, for remote / Java / C# servers that can't link native Rust:
  Rust engine → WASM component (WIT world) → batch → WS/IPC → remote driver
  (copying acceptable)
```

## The one thing to flag as

Okay...  So what I want is the same way to use the components build in rust for any language. But you are saying I can just use wit without using wasm? And then have zero-copy for any language when using fx. gtk driver.

Your understanding is exactly right, and this is the key architectural realization. Let me confirm it crisply:

**Yes — you can use WIT as the interface contract WITHOUT running the components in WASM.** And yes — that gives you zero-copy for any language with a native driver (GTK, AppKit, etc.).

## Why this works

The **WIT world is just a type/interface definition** — it does not mandate WASM. It says "here are the functions: `create-node(id, variant)`, `insert-child`, `set-property`, `begin-frame`, `emit`, `take-batch`, `dispatch`." Any host language that has bindings to those functions — via `wit-bindgen` generating **native** bindings — can call them.

The two things you were conflating are separable:

| | WASM component | Native (cdylib/lib) with WIT interface |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Rust compiled to `.wasm`, loaded in a runtime (wasmtime) | Rust compiled to a native lib, linked into the host app |
| Memory | Guest isolated → host **cannot** zero-copy | Host + Rust **same address space** → **zero-copy ring** |
| Cross-language surface | WIT world (flat, no per-component wrappers) | **Same** WIT world (flat, no per-component wrappers) |
| Bindings | `wit-bindgen` (Java/Swift/C#/...) | `wit-bindgen` (same!) |
